records.title: Online Hearing Voices Peer Support Groups: Assessing Feasibility and Acceptability Within UK National Health Service Settings
records.abstract: Background: User-led hearing voices groups (HVGs) have existed for the past 40 years, but little research has been conducted into if and how this approach can be implemented in statutory mental health settings, and whether they can be delivered effectively when held online. The aim of this study was to conduct a feasibility and acceptability trial of an online HVG for the UK National Health Service (NHS) users who hear voices, to inform a future larger-scale trial. Methods: A mixed-methods, nonrandomized feasibility study of an online HVG was conducted with 9 participants. Participants attended weekly online meetings for 6 months and completed measures of social connectedness, voice hearing, personal recovery, as well as semi-structured interviews, at baseline and postintervention (26-weeks). Primary outcomes were qualitative and quantitative assessments of feasibility and acceptability. Results: Thirty-eight participants were referred to the trial, 9 of whom were recruited (100% of the target sample). The trial had high retention (100%) and engagement (mean = 13.2 groups attended). Participants reported positive features of attending this digital intervention, with 85% reporting it was helpful to meet other voice hearers, that the group helped them make sense of voice hearing experiences, that they received positive messages about recovery, and that the group represented a form of support they could not get elsewhere. Discussion: The findings indicate it is feasible and acceptable to run an online HVG within an NHS setting. A larger trial is needed to further investigate the utility, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of running online HVGs in the NHS. Trial Registration: ISRCTN11873550.

records.title: Detecting Features of Interpersonal Difficulties in First-Person Accounts of Schizophrenia; Automated Linguistic and Network Analyses
records.abstract: Abstract Background First-person accounts (FPAs) provide multi-faceted insights into the lived social experiences of schizophrenia. We examined FPAs and third-person accounts (TPAs) using automated linguistic and network analyses to extract narrative patterns in relation to interpersonal difficulties. Study Design Narratives from 279 articles published in Schizophrenia Bulletin (1979-2025) were screened to identify 133 FPAs and 44 TPAs. Schizotypal Personality Questionnaire was used to assess syndromes of schizotypy expressed in the narratives. At least one cognitive-perceptual syndrome (ideas of reference, odd beliefs, magical thinking) was detected in every FPA (n = 133). Interpersonal difficulties (social anxiety, no close friends, constricted affect) were detected in 56 FPAs and designated as the “interpersonal difficulties” group. We used the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count software to extract interpersonally relevant features: authenticity, emotional tone, pronoun use, social behavior, and confidence. Linguistic features of narratives in FPAs with and without interpersonal difficulties were compared using network analysis. Study Results Greater authenticity and lower confidence were detected in FPAs compared to TPAs. FPAs contained fewer social words and more “I” words than TPAs. FPAs with interpersonal difficulties were longer, more negative, and less linguistically formal than FPAs without interpersonal difficulties. Network analysis indicated a link between interpersonal difficulties and “voices.” Conclusions Narratives categorized by interpersonal difficulties exhibit distinct linguistic signatures revealed through automated linguistic tools and network analyses. Despite the vast range of topics in FPAs, these computational methods provide a robust quantitative framework for validating the lived experience of negative syndrome in schizotypy.

records.title: The Lived Experience of Paranoia: Systematic Review of Qualitative Studies
records.abstract: Background and Hypothesis: Paranoia is commonly conceptualized along a continuum ranging from transient suspiciousness and mistrust to fixed persecutory delusions. However, similar paranoid contents may differ in conviction, flexibility, self-reference, distress, functional impact, and embeddedness in broader changes of self, agency, and world-experience. We synthesized qualitative evidence on the subjective experience of paranoia, suspiciousness, mistrust, and persecutory threat. Study Design: Following PRISMA and ENTREQ guidance, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Scopus, EBSCOhost, and Ovid from inception to January 31, 2026. Thirty-six qualitative, experiential, or mixed-methods studies were included. Data were analyzed using thematic synthesis informed by phenomenological principles. Studies were classified as core evidence when paranoia was central, or contextual evidence when paranoia-related material was embedded within broader phenomena. Study Results: Three superordinate themes were generated: From interpersonal vigilance to a persecutory world; The threatened self: shame, vulnerability, trauma, and social injury; and Restoring meaning and safety: agency, coping, and altered reality. Paranoia emerged not only as a belief about threat, but as a situated transformation in the relation between self, others, and world. Lower-severity and non-clinical accounts were generally more localized, reflective, and negotiable. Clinical and higher-severity accounts were more pervasive, embodied, self-referential, and reality-defining, often intertwined with voices, external control, altered agency, spiritual meanings, or changes in reality-experience. Conclusions: Paranoia is a multidimensional lived experience shaped by interpersonal threat, self-vulnerability, trauma, sociocultural context, coping, and meaning-making. Assessment should consider what paranoid beliefs mean, what they do for the person, and how they are shaped by biography, context, and lived experience.

records.title: Peer Support Work in Hospital: A First Person and Lived Experience Guide
records.abstract: People with mental health issues, like Ben, can find life daunting, frightening, isolating, disturbing, despairing, confusing, and even threatening. People can feel excluded, stigmatized, and left behind, in general life, education, employment, by health and social care services, and in research/evaluation. I myself have high anxiety in new situations and sometimes panic attacks, which make my heart flutter and cause nausea and dizziness. I have problems reading people’s non-verbal behavior and talking with more than one person because I hear voices. The antipsychotic medication I am on can make me feel very tired, lethargic, passive, tranquillized, and even zombie like. I have also heard voices with a hellish and demonic quality, saying: “You wait until you see what I’m going to do to you!!,” “Hot fire in your eyes,” and “On the bonfire with him!.” Too often, people can withdraw into themselves and be separated from others and society, living life on the margins and being labeled with the harmful concepts of psychosis and schizophrenia. People can become a shell and feel that they do not matter and are not valued. Ben’s experiences, and the experiences of other people with mental health issues, make a very strong case for involving people, in all aspects of life, health and social care services, education, and in employment such as peer support work. It is found in this article that peer support involves practical and emotional support and care work in mental health by drawing on the lived and personal experience and insight of Peer Support Workers (PSWs) in their interactions with people with mental health problems. This involves sharing experiences and stories in a hope filled and empathetic manner that explores people’s common humanity so as to overcome the challenges of mental health. Peer support enables working together to co-produce services and changing traditional relationships in hospital to improve models and practice in mental health care. The voice and lived experience of the person with mental health problems is heard and placed at the center of mental health services.1 As Repper describes peer support: It is through this trusting relationship, which offers companionship, empathy and empowerment, that feelings of isolation and rejection can be replaced with hope, a sense of agency and belief in personal control.1(p4) Peer support is when people use their own experiences to help each other. There are different types of peer support, but they all aim to bring together people with shared experiences to support each other, provide a space where people feel accepted and understood (MIND UK). This recovery-focused support often happens quite naturally as we meet others who have similar experiences—whether these experiences are social, familial, cultural, emotional, physical, or relate to mental health. Quite importantly, all PSWs have lived experience of mental illness, history of drug and alcohol addiction, as carers, learning disabilities, and dementia care and several have children with autism and special needs. The majority of PSWs are female, which reflects the gendered nature of care work. Rather than being a limitation, as this might be in most occupations, these qualities enable a tacit understanding of peer support work and better appreciation of peer support work’s core values, principles, and best practice, as described below. All PSWs in cohort one trained with Implementing Recovery through Organizational Change (ImROC. See: https://imroc.org). ImROC offers 10 principles and values of peer support: 1 Mutuality: Connection based on mutual understanding, and empathy. 2 Reciprocity: Both parties give and gain in a peer support relationship. People take turns and give and take. 3 Non-directive: Interaction and dialogue is guided by the person with mental health problems. PSWs support people to find their own solutions. 4 Recovery Focused: Inspiring hope, giving back control, identifying opportunities. 5 Trauma informed: Understanding that trauma needs to be recognized, dealt with and that it can impact people differently. 6 Strengths Based: Helping people to identify their strengths and build on them. 7 Inclusive: Of all people from different communities, ethnicities, sexualities, and backgrounds. 8 Progressive: Focusing on the progressive steps through recovery. 9 Safe: Ensuring that all parties have feelings of safety and a safe environment. 10 Equitable: Making sure that peer support is accessible to all. There are two main methods: A reflective journal was kept that documented experiences and interactions on the ward. Participant observation was conducted and noted in the reflective journal. There is a lot of literature on peer support in mental health but relatively little conducted on inpatient mental health units by people with lived experience of mental illness. This means that this account is innovative and perhaps even unique. It uncovers a hidden and first-person narrative on the nature of peer support. Drawing from the reflective journal, peer support work is found to be highly therapeutic, positive, and valued by people experiencing mental health problems. In particular, sharing stories and experiences of mental illness with people leads to trust, feelings of being heard, and accepted. It also results in a better experience of care and being seen as a person first (being trauma informed and not diagnosis lead). Peer support offers hope of progressive recovery and feelings of safety in an inpatient environment that can sometimes be experienced as distressing, lethargic, boring, despairing, and even hostile. One person described the ward as “hell” and “you never know what’s going on,” this demonstrates how difficult a mental inpatient environment can be for both staff and people with mental health problems. However, he went on to say: “The PSWs listen to me. They helped me find out if I was on Section or informal and talked about getting me escorted leave. I feel like they can understand what I’m going through.” PSWs are able to befriend people with mental health problems based on mutuality and human connection. Importantly the working relationship between peers is reciprocal, as in both parties gain something, and is beneficial in terms of the PSW’s own recovery journey. This mutual connection through lived experience establishes rapport, whilst being trauma informed and adhering to the core values of peer support (ImROC). However, there is still a need to be clear on professional boundaries meaning that people are not seen as friends but rather as mentors and mentees. At times PSWs can struggle with this, largely due to the need to connect on a human level based on mutual experiences, however, it is vital to maintain the connectedness between peers to add value to the experience of care. It is important to note that PSWs are not there to diagnose or treat, they are non-directive and non-judgmental (ImROC), therefore this creates a psychologically safe space for people to share, engage, and discuss without fear. This connectivity appears to be missing currently as services can feel quite transactional. A minority of health staff can be disconnected, lacking empathy toward people with mental health problems on the ward. Staff are sometimes preoccupied with observation and administration over therapeutic engagement. This is perhaps not surprising given the long shifts of staff, the number of tasks asked of them, and their sometimes limited training in trauma-informed care, and the recovery approach and model. Conversely, people in services see the staff providing care as faceless and dehumanize them, seeing the transactional processes and systems as being unable to meet their needs. This sentiment can create a hostile environment and can result in those in care acting violently and aggressively toward staff, which often escalates to restraint and restrictive practice. PSWs can bridge this gap between staff and people with mental health problems. For PSWs their work is a vocation that they are passionate about and in which they have personal insight. PSWs help compensate for understaffing and provide high-quality care and support that has received positive feedback (see below). PSWs fulfill many of the jobs that other staff are unable to do because they lack sufficient time. For example, taking people on escorted leave when staff are too busy, empowering people to self-advocate, advocating for people when they have felt unable to themselves, providing therapeutic engagement, assisting with ward reviews and discharge, facilitating peer groups, being an empathetic ear actively listening as a person talks through their recovery, and many more as listed below in the themes. In the feedback of two people with mental health problems on the ward: I haven’t experienced anything as good as peer support before. And I have been in hospital a lot over the years. I usually become psychotic about once every three years. The PSWs take you out and about to have some time away from the chaos of the ward. They have personal insight, unlike other staff, and they have experience of mental illness. I feel like PSWs listen to me and understand my perspective more than the other staff. My PSWs said I should try art therapy, which I enjoyed, found relaxing, and was less stress than being on the ward. I give the peer support team 10 out of 10. There’s no need for feedback. My three words to describe peer support are: “You are brilliant!.” Thanks for caring for us. The main themes from the reflective journal include: Feelings of being listened to, valued, accepted, heard, understood, and worthwhile. Better experiences and satisfaction with care. Promoting a safe environment and feelings of safety. Assisting with ward reviews, Mental Health Tribunals and appeals. Leading and encouraging people to engage in ward activities. Encouraging adherence to medication. Assisting with discharge and freeing up beds. Insight into hearing voices, seeing things (hallucinations), and unusual thoughts or beliefs (delusions). Encouraging people to focus on their strengths and positives and build upon them. Encouraging people’s skills and goals to offer a future in which recovery is planned for and achievable. Calming people having a panic attack. De-escalating situations, intervening, and preventing need for restraint by staff. Also preventing aggression/violence between people on the ward and toward staff Listening and developing coping strategies and insight into trauma. Deflecting/preventing suicidal thoughts. Raising awareness of LGBTQ+ issues among staff (and in their interactions with LGBTQ+ people on the ward). Encouraging drug/alcohol cessation. The benefit of PSWs taking people on escorted leave (especially when staff are too busy). Supporting people with unescorted leave, especially helpful for those who are anxious of going out alone. Encouraging physical exercise (walking, dance, football, table tennis, basketball, etc.). Encouraging people to eat and self-care. Empowering people to think about and resolve issues at home in a practical and pragmatic way. Supporting staff when they feel overwhelmed. Peer support acts as a form of social and emotional support with people with mental health problems. This is a vital and therapeutic connection between people that requires openness, dialogue, and conversation with others, emotional honesty, empathy, philanthropy, or caring for other people’s feelings and experiences on a journey toward recovery. Peer support work opens a space for communication, reciprocity, mutuality, and dialogue between people about their shared experiences of mental health problems and distress. This time, both the person with mental health problems and peer worker realize that they are not alone but undergoing a shared experience and journey toward better mental health. You get back what you give to other people: such as support, care, kindness, and even a bit of love. PSWs shine a light in the darkness of mental illness and stop it from consuming them, inspiring hope. In addition, psychosis is sometimes perceived as something frightening, wrong, untoward, and “dirty.” For PSWs it is an understandable experience, not a diagnosis or harmful label. The findings provide rich and convincing evidence that peer support is highly therapeutic, complimenting the existing and sometimes stretched ward establishment. It is a worthwhile investment for all inpatient services and promotes people’s journey of recovery from mental illness and trauma-informed care. Peer support work is an important innovation that can be scaled up to other healthcare providers, and should be a staple of any ward establishment because of the benefits it brings to both staff and people with mental health problems. However, it is important to note that the peer support role can be hugely demanding, asking people to connect empathetically to their lived experience and support others as peers. It is therefore vitally important to ensure that the people who take up this role are appropriately trained, supported, and supervised. Therefore, supervision relies on the supervision triangle of “restoration,” “reflection,” and “development” and PSWs trained with ImROC. According to Repper,1 and in our own personal experience, PSWs feel empowered in their own recovery journey, have greater confidence and self-esteem, and a more positive sense of identity. They feel less self-stigmatization, have more skills, more money, and feel more valued. Being employed as a peer worker is generally seen as a positive and safe way to re-enter the job market and thus resume a key social and professional role. Finally, it is important to highlight barriers to peer support. These include: 1 Over-sedation on antipsychotic and antidepressant medication creates a barrier to interaction, communication, and dialogue. 2 Ben felt guilty and as though he had let down people with mental health problems on the ward when he finished his shift and left for home. He often felt stressed with headaches after a shift. Ben had a long commute to the ward but found peer support very rewarding. There is the need for supervision to manage these emotions, which was provided to Ben by Matt. Ben was also buddied with another PSW and PSWs were allowed to do flexible shifts and reduced hours to better manage negative experiences and feelings. 3 Peer support can be “discontinuous” or “fractured.” In other words, you establish a rapport and befriend the person with mental health problems. You then assist in their recovery and discharge from hospital. New people arrive on the ward and you have to start the whole process again. This is a bit like going back to square one and a broken relationship that must be coped with during team meetings, buddying, and supervision. 4 One person on the ward often called staff “Mum” and “Dad.” On one occasion he called a member of staff. “Mum.” “He called you mum,” I said to the member of staff. “I know,” she said. “That’s why I’m ignoring him.” A fine balance is required so as not to ignore or feed into someone’s psychosis, which is an everyday dilemma and occurrence on a mental health ward. 5 In Ben’s view, there tends to be an “Us” and “Them” atmosphere, culture, and mentality between staff and people with mental health problems. PSWs must win the trust of both groups which is a delicate balance. PSWs bridge the gap, belonging and encouraging dialogue between staff and people with mental health problems on the ward. 6 PSWs need to be aware of power imbalances and ready to advocate for and empower people with mental health problems. This first-person account and lived experience perspective expresses the views of the first author (Ben). It does not necessarily reflect the views of the co-author (Matt), the Peer Support Team or the NHS Trust. For further information on becoming a Peer Support Worker email: [email protected]. The authors would like to thank the Peer Support Team and other colleagues. Many thanks to Renee, Rosario, Charlotte, Olivia, Liz, and Lauren.

records.title: Diglossia Correlates With Prodromal Symptoms of Psychosis Among First-Generation Migrants
records.abstract: Background and Hypothesis: We have previously hypothesized that diglossia may be a risk factor for psychosis, drawing from observations on migration, ethnicity, social adversity, and language disturbances among others. However, empirical data on this association and the tools necessary for its measurement are limited. Study Design: In a cross-sectional online sample of first-generation migrants residing in majority English-speaking countries, a response-based decision tree was introduced to classify the sociolinguistic profiles of 1497 participants as either with or without diglossia. Using multivariate logistic regression, the association of diglossia with psychosis risk screening outcomes in the Prodromal Questionnaire-16 was calculated, adjusting for demographic and linguistic confounders. Differences in the symptom categories endorsed between the 2 groups were also examined. Study Results: Diglossia was identified in 18.4% of participants and was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.58 for a positive risk screening outcome. Other significant factors included subjective social status, hearing difficulty, age, sex, country of residence, education level, and cannabis consumption. The effects of ethnicity, age at migration, fluency, relationship, and employment status were no more significant in the multivariate model. Finally, the largest differences in the proportion of positively responding participants between the two groups were found in symptoms relating to thought insertion and thought broadcasting. Conclusions: In a sociolinguistic hierarchical framework, diglossia is correlated with prodromal symptoms of psychosis in first-generation migrants.
